issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette:
Kwame is a 62-year-old African American man who has spent the better part of four decades working in bomb disposal, a career he describes with quiet pride as a calling rather than a job. He is married, the father of grown children, and until approximately fourteen months ago, he was a man who, by his own account, had learned to live comfortably inside danger. What he had not prepared for was the particular kind of danger that came without a visible device, without a timer, without anything he could disarm.

The incident occurred during a routine inspection of an abandoned industrial facility that had been flagged as a potential site for an improvised explosive cache. Kwame and a colleague entered a sub-basement storage room where, without warning, they were enveloped by a release of toxic chemical vapour from corroded industrial containers. The smell hit first - acrid, synthetic, coating the back of the throat - and within seconds Kwame's vision blurred and his legs gave out beneath him. He remembers the concrete floor against his cheek, the sound of his colleague shouting somewhere above him, and then the prolonged, disorienting hours that followed in hospital: the antiseptic sting of the ward, the bright overhead lights, the sensation of his body having become something unreliable and alien. He was discharged after several days, told the acute effects had resolved, and returned to modified duties within weeks. What did not resolve was something harder to name.

In the months that followed, Kwame began to notice that certain things undid him in ways he could neither predict nor explain to his satisfaction. Walking into any part of his workplace - the equipment bay, the briefing room, even the car park - would bring on a wave of physical agitation that he described as his body preparing for something terrible before his mind had caught up. Loud noises, which his career had long since habituated him to, now landed differently; a door slamming in the corridor would send him rigid, his hands braced against whatever surface was nearest. And the smell of antiseptic - encountered in a supermarket cleaning aisle, in a colleague's first aid kit, at a routine dental appointment - would stop him cold in a way he found deeply disorienting and, he admitted with some difficulty, frightening.

Kwame had come to believe, in a way that felt less like a thought than a physical fact, that his body was still compromised in ways the doctors had missed or had not told him. He was certain that remaining still, remaining alone, remaining unoccupied was when the damage would make itself known. And so he did not remain still. He began taking on additional shifts, volunteering for every available tasking, filling his evenings with paperwork and equipment checks long after his colleagues had gone home. His wife, Adaeze, told him she felt she was living with someone who was always about to leave the room. He understood what she meant but could not stop. Being alone in the house - even briefly, even in the afternoon - produced a vigilance in him that he described as unbearable, a sense that something was converging on him from just outside his awareness.

In any new space - a restaurant, a waiting room, a relative's home - Kwame found himself conducting a quiet, systematic survey before he could settle: where the exits were, which chairs faced the door, whether the windows opened. He did this without deciding to. He also stopped scheduling the annual medical review his role required, finding reasons to defer it, and he had not returned to the hospital where he had been treated. The smell of that place, he felt, would confirm something he was not ready to know.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a single event but an accumulation. Adaeze told him, with a steadiness he recognised as the edge of her patience, that she was worried he had disappeared inside himself. And his unit commander, noting the excessive hours and a recent incident in which Kwame had reacted with visible alarm when a trainee placed a hand on his shoulder, had quietly suggested he speak to someone. Kwame arrived at his first session guarded but present. What he said he most feared was finding out that the exposure had changed him permanently. What he said he most hoped for, in almost the same breath, was that it hadn't.
